chunks: "I'd start by asking what volume, what defects we're most worried about, and what test stations the factory already has.
Then I plan test at layout time, because it's mostly about access.

For a bed-of-nails station, I'd give every net that matters a test pad on one side of the board, at least about 1 mm in size on a grid and spacing that the fixture vendor can probe, away from tall parts, no solder mask on it.
I'd keep power and ground pads spread across the board so there's a clean return for each region.
For nets I can't reach, like dense BGA signals, I'd use boundary scan, so the chips themselves become the test pins.

For functional test I'd add a test mode and a simple interface, like a UART or USB port, so the station can command the board, read self-test results and program calibration data without special hardware.
I'd also design the programming path so firmware flashes in-circuit through pads or a connector.
Then I'd do the math: test seconds per board times annual volume gives the number of stations, and fixture cost divided by volume is the per-board cost.
And I'd log every result with the serial number so we can track yield and catch drift early."
